per.notes: The report got the core story right. The portal was the way in, the CFO's month-end close was the real trigger, and a value case built from her own data took the deal from 20% to won. It kept the exact dollar figure and Fiserv's pitch as unknown. Its main miss is the header: it leaves the competitor field null even though Fiserv was both the competitor and the incumbent. It also leaves the counter-reader demo and the finance-language shift out of the formal messaging changes, though both appear in the sections.

fails: Decider insight puts a first-person quote, 'it was my call', in Maya's mouth. The transcript only has the rep's report: "She said it was her call." This is a reconstructed quote that does not appear in the transcript.
per.notes: Strong report. It carries the online-only scope note, surfaces the Maya-chose/Greg-decided contradiction, labels 'a third' as unverified, marks customer language Not covered, and points every messaging change at the key's direction using real excerpts. Main miss: the rep takeaway covers only finding the signer early. It never says to treat the front desk as a live, incumbent-held deal. The messaging also only implies, and never states, adding a live in-environment reader demo as the proof to build.

fails: Gaps insight puts a paraphrase in quotation marks as if it were the rep's words: 'work through it in implementation'. The transcript says "we'd work through the details in implementation".
per.notes: The report's strongest move is in the gaps section: it shows the rep's "clean" answer being contradicted by the unanswered Venmo question and the saved-card reference that was promised but never sent. It also keeps the Braintree theory clearly labeled as the rep's guess. Its weaknesses are small: the marketplace reaction is labeled opinion while similar rep observations are labeled fact, the message section says the auth-rate slide 'failed' rather than reporting the silence (that only appears in the messaging changes), and the close never asks whether PayPal/Venmo were resolved now that implementation has started.

The report's strongest point is the decider contradiction: it separates Raj's process role from Angela's signature, the workshop her team requested and the rep's single meeting with her. It also ties 'that's a diagram' to a demonstrated till-return message. It missed the incumbent (separate store and web providers, implied by the split customer records) and listed it as an open question instead. It mislabelled the December 27 Angela story as opinion when it is secondhand fact, and its close omits the key's open questions about what Bev wrote down and whether a named rollout plan would have been accepted. The rep's T28 'better product online' is never cited, so it is not misused, but it is also not explicitly labelled as opinion.

fails: Trigger section states the engineering manager 'valued developer experience'. The transcript does not say this.
Decider section asserts 'nobody at Stripe ever reached the CFO'. The transcript does not establish this.
Decided section uses the interviewer's question 'Had you met Stefan before the renewal?' as an evidence excerpt labelled 'fact'.
Trigger section labels 'He mentioned Brazil and a couple in Europe. I never saw his analysis.' as fact. The key requires opinion/unverified.
per.notes: The report strongly challenges 'decided before we got in the room' using the coverage facts: no business review for 9–10 months, never met Stefan, learned of the evaluation from the renewal notice, and an analysis that was late but valued. It also keeps the Adyen results unknown and turns 'what's mine?' into a customer-specific-numbers messaging change. Its main misses are the tag, where it chose Value proof and put Approval rates only as runner-up, and the Our-message section. That section never cites the 'average' quotes as evidence and drifts to roadmap silence instead of concluding that average-uplift messaging fails with a sophisticated payments buyer. It also mislabels the unverified markets as fact.

The report gets the core story right. The CTO champion won the technical evaluation, and the COO decided on 'who picks up.' Its messaging changes (names over tiers, an on-sale plan, people-based references) are evidence-backed, and it labels 'over-promised' as unverified opinion. It misses three things: it leaves competitor and incumbent null, which the transcript does not name either, so it rightly flags them as unknowns; it frames the on-sale plan as partly a product or packaging gap when both gaps were closable by the team in the room; and it labels Halima's 'good.' as a quote where the key treats it as fact.

Strong report. It correctly calls this Value proof, not price, and shows the rep undercutting his own price claim (IT nervous before spring; 'same rate, so why move'). It also surfaces the skipped decline analysis, the unanswered business-case request and the rate-only comparison page, and its messaging changes match all four expected directions using real transcript evidence. Weaknesses: the 'decided' section never cites the rep's 'more room on the rate, we win this' line as opinion (the opinion label sits on 'We lost on price' in the message section); the trigger insight skips that the pain was owned by someone who couldn't sign; and the close never lists the dollar value of failed orders as an explicit open item or recommends offering the decline analysis now, ahead of spring.

The report gets the core story right: the portal was the way in and the CFO's month-end close was the reason, a value case built from her own data won the deal, Fiserv's pitch stays unknown, and no specific dollar figure appears. Every excerpt is verbatim, and the messaging changes follow all four expected directions. It misses one open question the key names, whether the 14 branch counter readers are in scope, and replaces it with a 'why us' question. It also labels the inbound portal evidence as opinion when the key treats it as fact.

The report gets the central story right. It scopes 'Won' to online memberships, with Global still at the front desk and phase two undated. It surfaces the Maya-chose/Greg-decided contradiction, and it ties the win to failed-payment recovery shown on the customer's own file, with clean quote/fact/opinion labels throughout. Its main miss is the rep takeaway: it covers 'find whose signature is needed earlier' but drops the key's other half, treating the front desk as a live competitive deal rather than a done one. It also makes one minor unsupported claim, 'our messaging so far has been aimed at Maya's concerns', which the transcript does not establish.

The report gets the core story right. It surfaces the Raj-to-Angela contradiction, ties 'that's a diagram' to replacing the claim with a live till-return demo, and points every messaging change in the key's direction (customer language, rollout capability, a callable reference). Its main misses are in the header and close. The incumbent is left null and then listed as an unknown, although the transcript implies separate store and web systems. None of the key's not-covered items appear (Adyen's terms, what Bev wrote down, whether a partner-install rollout plan would have been accepted). The December 27th COO story is labelled opinion rather than secondhand fact, and 'better product online' (T28) is never addressed directly, only implicitly through 'winning the web side did not matter'.

The report gets the core of the deal right. The tech champion (Ben) differs from the COO decider (Halima), and "queue with a faster timer" drives a names-not-tiers messaging change. Over-promised is correctly labeled opinion, and the four messaging directions all appear with verbatim evidence. It misses the key's competitor and incumbent, though neither Checkout.com nor the in-house gateway appears in this transcript, so the 0 reflects the key, not a reasoning error. It also moves 'what decided it' away from the 'queue' sentence and toward the missing plan, and its close omits the named on-sale coverage follow-up and wrongly calls the gaps question 'dodged'.

The report correctly overturns the rep's 'lost on price' story. It shows that the CFO saw only a rate-vs-rate page and our quote, that 'the same thing' was a differentiation failure, and that the rep turned down Farah's decline analysis. Its messaging changes track all four expected directions with real excerpts. It misses some details. It mislabels the 'no new product' point about the incumbent as opinion when it is fact per Lucy. The trigger insight never says the pain was owned by someone who couldn't sign. The close neither lists 'what the failed orders were worth' as never calculated nor suggests offering the decline analysis now, ahead of spring.

The report gets the core story right. It treats the payback request a month before the freeze as the turning point, shows that the generic ROI deck failed against 'a number that's ours', and does not accept 'timing' as the whole story. Its messaging changes match the key's direction well. However, it uses Value proof as the tag instead of No decision. It challenges the rep's 'nothing we could have done' but never cites it as labelled opinion evidence. The close leaves out the key's 'not covered' item (what the homegrown system actually costs) and the follow-ups for a migration reference and renewal-season timing.

The report gets the core right: it tags Value proof, rejects the 'lost on price' framing because the CFO saw only rate lines next to our quote, and surfaces Farah's declined three-month decline analysis and Lucy's unmet request for a business case. It never quotes the rep's closing claim, 'If we'd had more room on the rate, we win this', so it does not label that claim as opinion in the decided section. It labels the related 'We lost on price' as opinion only in the message section. Its close also omits 'what the failed orders were worth' as an open question and the follow-up of offering the decline analysis ahead of spring. Its fourth messaging change (drop the M6 ROI claim) rests on no evidence in the transcript.
